extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in comedy history, improvisation, and Elaine May
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria about the performance and writing techniques used by Nichols and May and Elaine May individually — especially scene-based improvisation, character work, and satirical subject selection. Useful for performers, students of comedy, or historians analyzing mid‑20th century American improv and sketch work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene-based performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Their stage performance created "scenes," a method very unlike the styles of other acting teams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor developing short dramatic situations between characters (scenes) rather than relying on one‑liner jokes or set comic bit structures; aim to make each sketch feel like a self-contained scene with character interaction and stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Snob and mob appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: They used both "snob and mob appeal," which gave them a wide audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance material so it contains intellectual or sophisticated references ('snob' appeal) while still remaining accessible and broadly relatable ('mob' appeal). This broadens audience reach without sacrificing subtlety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexible character roles (no fixed comic roles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nor did they rely on fixed gender or comic roles, but instead adapted their own character to fit a sketch idea they came up with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid pigeonholing performers into a single stock role (e.g., 'straight man' or 'dumb sidekick'); instead vary character types to serve the scene and explore different dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use real-life subjects and satirize everyday life
rubrics_metrics.description: They chose real-life subjects, often from their own life, which were made into satirical and funny vignettes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mine familiar, everyday situations for satire; grounding sketches in recognizable realities increases audience recognition and comedic payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtle joke references expecting audience recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: This was accomplished by using subtle joke references which they correctly expected their audiences to recognize, whether through clichés or character types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on understatement and implication rather than explicit punchlines; trust the audience's cultural literacy to catch indirect or layered jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvisation as situation + problem
rubrics_metrics.description: According to May: "It's nothing more than quickly creating a situation between two people and throwing up some kind of problem for one of them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When improvising, focus on establishing a clear situation and then introduce a problem or obstacle — the scene should emerge from how characters react to that problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediacy and minimal rehearsal for freshness
rubrics_metrics.description: They would perform a sketch soon after coming up with the idea with little extra rehearsal or writing it down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor quick realization of ideas and preserve spontaneity; avoid over‑polishing early improvisations which can drain the initial impulse and energy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of structure and exploratory play
rubrics_metrics.description: Nichols always needed to know where a sketch was going and what its ultimate point would be, while May preferred exploring ideas as the scene progressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine a guiding structure (an arc or endpoint) with openness to exploration; one collaborator can shape/steer while another expands possibilities in the moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break gender stereotypes in role selection
rubrics_metrics.description: May helped remove the stereotype of women's roles on stage by not choosing traditional 1950s female roles and often playing sophisticated women (doctor, psychiatrist, employer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately cast and write women in varied, non‑stereotypical roles to subvert expectations and expand comedic possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rote repetition — keep material fresh
rubrics_metrics.description: Keeping their act fresh was becoming more difficult; repeated material took a great toll on performers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure routines evolve and avoid repeating the same beats or sketches verbatim; refresh material to maintain performer engagement and audience surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncovering 'little dark niches' — reveal unspoken feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: They would "uncover little dark niches that you felt but had never expressed," producing surprising, resonant comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to expose small, often unspoken emotional truths or anxieties in a way that makes audiences both recognize and laugh at them — comedy that reveals shared inner life can be especially powerful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirize contemporary banalities and relationships ('Age of Irony')
rubrics_metrics.description: Nichols and May created a new 'Age of Irony' for comedy, which showed actors arguing contemporary banalities as a key part of their routine; they were among the first to satirize relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target the mundanity and social rituals of contemporary life (including relationship dynamics) for satire; framing trivial arguments or social conventions as the subject of comedic scrutiny can be fertile ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nuanced characterizations and 'cultured types'
rubrics_metrics.description: Their work featured "nuances of the characterizations and the cultured types" appealing to performers like Lily Tomlin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop characters with subtle, specific traits and social/cultural markers (the 'cultured type') rather than broad caricatures; nuanced portrayals yield richer comedic textures.
